readings.c1s1:
¶
'''topgallant''' (top′gal″ant; by sailors usually to-gal′ant), ''a.'' and ''n.'' I. ''a.'' 1. Being above the topmast and below the royal: applied to mast, sail, rigging, etc.—2†. Topping; fine.

{{smaller block|''Top-gallant'' he, and she in all her trim.
{{right|''Pope'', Satires of Donne, iv. 230.}}}}

II. ''n.'' 1. The topgallant mast, sail, or rigging of a ship.

{{smaller block|A goodly ship with banners bravely dight,
And flag in her ''top-gallant'', I espide.
{{right|''Spenser'', Visions of the World's Vanity, l. 100.}}}}

2. Figuratively, any elevated part, place, etc.

{{smaller block|And bring thee cords made like a tackled stair;
Which to the high ''top-gallant'' of my joy
Must be my convoy in the secret night.
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., ii. 4. 202.}}}}

'''Rolling topgallantsail.''' See ''rolling.''—'''Top and topgallant.''' See ''top''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Topgallant-bulwarks.''' See ''quarter-board.''—'''Topgallant-forecastle.''' See ''forecastle.''—'''Topgallant-shrouds.''' See ''shroud''<sup>2</sup>.

'''top-graining''' (top′grā″ning), ''n.'' An additional coating of color, either in distemper or in oil, put over the first coat of graining after it is dry.

'''toph''' (tof), ''n.'' In ''surg.'', same as ''tophus.''

'''tophaceous''' (tō-fā′shius), ''a.'' [< ''toph'' + ''-aceous.''] Pertaining to a toph or tophus; gritty; sandy: as, a ''tophaceous'' concretion.

{{smaller block|It [milk] differs from a vegetable emulsion by coagulating into a curdy mass with acids, which chyle and vegetable emulsions will not. Acids mixed with them precipitate a ''tophaceous'' chalky matter, but not a chyly substance.
{{right|''Arbuthnot'', Aliments, IV. ii. § 4.}}}}
readings.c1s2:
¶ '''top-hamper''' (top′ham″pėr), ''n.'' ''Naut.'': (''a'') Any unnecessary weight, either aloft or about the upper decks. {{smaller block|So encumbered with ''top-hamper'', so over-weighted in proportion to their draught of water. {{right|''Motley.'' (''Imp. Dict.'')}}}} (''b'') The light upper sails and their gear. (''c'') The whole of the rigging and sails of a ship. [Rare.] '''top-hampered''' (top′ham″pėrd), ''a.'' Having too much weight aloft; hence, top-heavy. '''top-heaviness''' (top′hev″i-nes), ''n.'' The state of being top-heavy. ''Jour. Franklin Inst.'', CXXVI. 178. '''top-heavy''' (top′hev″i), ''a.'' 1. Having the top disproportionately heavy; over-weighted at the top. {{smaller block|Like trees that broadest sprout,
Their own ''top-heavy'' state grubs up their root. {{right|''Chapman'', Byron's Conspiracy, iii. 1.}}}} 2. Figuratively, lacking fitness of proportions; liable to fall or fail. {{smaller block|The scheme has become more ''top-heavy'', in that the pensions for the aged or disabled workmen are graded, varying according to the wages they have been earning. {{right|''The Nation'', XLVIII. 377.}}}} 3. Drunk; tipsy. ''Leland.'' [Slang.] '''Tophet''' (tō′fet), ''n.'' [< Heb. ''tōpheth'', lit. a place to be spit on, < ''túph'', spit.] A place situated at the southeastern extremity of Gehenna, or Valley of Hinnom, to the south of Jerusalem. {{smaller block|It was there that the idolatrous Jews worshiped the fire-gods and sacrificed their children. In consequence of these abominations the whole valley became the common laystall of the city, and symbolical of the place of torment in a future life.}}
readings.c1s3:
The pleasant valley of Hinnom, ''Tophet'' thence
And black Gehenna call'd, the type of hell.
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., i. 404.}}}}

¶
'''tophi''', ''n.'' Plural of ''tophus''.

'''top-honors†''' (top′on″o̤rz), ''n.'' Topsails. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|As our high Vessels pass their wat'ry Way,
Let all the naval World due Homage pay;
With hasty Reverence their ''Top-honours'' lower.
{{right|''Prior'', Carmen Seculare, 1700, st. 36.}}}}

'''tophus''' (tō′fus), ''n.''; pl. ''tophi'' (-fī). [< L. ''tophus'', ''tofus'', sandstone: see ''tufa'', ''tuff''<sup>3</sup>.] A concretion of calcareous matter which forms on the cartilaginous surface of the joints, and on the pinna of the ear, in gout; a gouty deposit.

'''topi''', '''topee''' (tō-pē′), ''n.'' In India, a hat or cap. {{smaller|—'''Sola''' or '''solar topi.''' See ''sola''<sup>2</sup>.}}

'''topia''' (tō′pi-ä̤), ''n.'' [L., landscape-gardening, landscape-painting, neut. pl. (sc. ''opera'') of *''topius'', < ''topos'', < Gr. τόπος, a place: see ''topic''.] A fanciful style of mural decoration, generally consisting of landscapes of a very heterogeneous character, resembling those of the Chinese, much used in ancient Roman houses.

'''topiarian''' (tō-pi-ā′ri-an), ''a.'' [< L. ''topiarius'', topiary, + ''-an''.] Of, pertaining to, or practising topiary work.

{{smaller block|Clipped yews and hollies, and all the pedantries of the ''topiarian'' art.
{{right|''Kingsley'', Westward Ho, vii.}}}}

'''topiary''' (tō′pi-ạ̄-ri), ''a.'' [< L. ''topiarius'', an ornamental or landscape gardener, < ''topia'', landscape-gardening: see ''topia''.] In ''gardening'', clipped or cut into ornamental shapes; also, of
readings.c3s3:
¶
'''top-lantern''' (top′lan″tėrn), ''n.'' ''Naut.'', a large lantern carried in the mizzentop of a flag-ship, from which a light is displayed as a designation on the admiral's ship.

'''topless''' (top′les), ''a.'' [< ''top''<sup>1</sup> + ''-less.''] Having no top; immeasurably high; lofty; preëminent; exalted.

{{smaller block|Was this the face that launched a thousand ships, And burnt the ''topless'' towers of Ilium?
{{right|''Marlowe'', Dr. Faustus, xiv.}}}}

{{smaller block|Make their strengths totter, and their ''topless'' fortunes Unroot, and reel to ruin!
{{right|''Fletcher'', Bonduca, iii. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|''Topless'' honours be bestow'd on thee.
{{right|''Chapman'', Blind Beggar of Alexandria.}}}}

'''top-light''' (top′līt), ''n.'' A light kept in the top of a ship for signaling or for the use of the topmen.

'''top-lining''' (top′lī″ning), ''n.'' ''Naut.'': (''a'') The lining on the after part of the topsail, to prevent the top-rim from chafing the topsail. (''b'') A platform of thin board nailed upon the upper part of the crosstrees on a vessel's top.

'''toploftical''' (top′lôf″ti-kal), ''a.'' [< ''toplofty'' + ''-ical.''] Toplofty. [Colloq., U. S.]

{{smaller block|The ecclesiastical [party] who do the ''toploftical'' talking, and make the inflammatory speeches in the Tabernacle.
{{right|''The Congregationalist'', Dec. 17, 1879.}}}}
readings.c3s4:
¶
'''toploftiness''' (top′lôf″ti-nes), ''n.'' The character of being toplofty. [Colloq., U. S.]

'''toplofty''' (top′lôf″ti), ''a.'' Having a high top; hence, figuratively, pompous; bombastic; inflated; pretentious: as, ''toplofty'' airs; ''toplofty'' speeches. [Colloq., U. S.]

'''top-mall''' (top′mâl), ''n.'' See ''mall''<sup>1</sup>.

'''topman''' (top′man), ''n.''; pl. ''topmen'' (-men). [< ''top''<sup>1</sup> + ''man.''] 1. The man who stands above in sawing; a top-sawyer.—2. ''Naut.'', a man stationed to do duty in a top. In a man-of-war the topmen are divided into fore-, main-, and mizzen-topmen. Also ''topsman.''—3. A merchant vessel. ''Halliwell.''

[< L. ''topiarius'', an ornamental or landscape gardener, < ''topia'', landscape-gardening: see ''topia''.] In ''gardening'', clipped or cut into ornamental shapes; also, of or pertaining to such trimming. Topiary work is the clipping and trimming of trees and shrubs into regular or fantastic shapes. {{smaller block|I was lead to a pretty garden, planted with hedges of alaternus, having at the entrance a skreene at an exceeding height, accurately cutt in ''topiary'' worke. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, March 25, 1644.}}}} '''topic''' (top′ik), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [I. ''a.'' Formerly also ''topick'', ''topique''; < F. ''topique'' = Sp. ''tópico'' = Pg. It. ''topico'', topic, local (in med. use), < NL. ''topicus'', local, < Gr. τοπικός, pertaining to a place, local, pertaining to a common place, or topic, topical, < τόπος, a place. II. ''n.'' Formerly also ''topick'', ''topique'', usually in pl.; < F. ''topique'', pl. ''topiques'', = Sp. ''tópica'' = Pg. It. ''topica'', < L. ''topica'', neut. pl., the title of a work of Aristotle, < Gr. τοπικά (τὰ τοπικά, the books concerning τόποι, or common places), neut. pl. of τοπικός, pertaining to a place: see I.] '''I.''' ''a.'' Local: same as ''topical''. {{smaller block|O all ye ''Topick'' Gods, that do inhabit here. {{right|''Drayton'', Polyolbion, xxx. 221.}}}} {{smaller block|The places ought, before the application of those ''topicke'' medicines, to be well prepared with the razour. {{right|''Holland'', tr. of Pliny, xxix. 6.}}}} '''II.''' ''n.'' 1. In ''logic'' and ''rhet.'', a common place (which see, under ''common''); a class of considerations from which probable arguments can be drawn. {{smaller|According to the opinion of some writers, the statements of Aristotle are only consistent with making a topic, or common place, a maxim of reasoning. The traditional definition coming through Cicero is "the seat of an argument." This is not very explicit, and the word has not commonly been used with a very rigid accuracy in logic or rhetoric. The chief topics concern the arguments from notation, conjugates, definition, genus, species, whole, part, cause, effect, subject, adjunct, disparates, contraries, relates, privatives, contradictories, greater, less, equals, similars, dissimilars, and testimony; but different logicians enumerate the topics differently.}} {{smaller block|The great arguments of Christianity against the practice of sin are not drawn from any uncertain ''Topicks,'' or nice and curious speculations. {{right|''Stillingfleet,'' Sermons, II. iii.}}}} 2. The subject of a discourse, argument, or literary composition, or the subject of any distinct part of a discourse, etc.; any matter treated of: now the usual meaning of the word. {{smaller block|It often happens . . . that the poet and the senate of Rome have both chosen the same ''topic'' to flatter their emperor upon, and have sometimes fallen upon the same thought. {{right|''Addison,'' Ancient Medals, i.}} Deem'st thou not our later time Yields ''topic'' meet for classic rhyme? {{right|''Scott,'' Marmion, iii., Int.}}}} 3. In ''med.'', a remedy locally applied. {{smaller block|Amongst ''topics'' or outward medicines, none are more precious than baths. {{right|''Burton,'' Anat. of Mel., p. 418.}}}} '''Transcendental topic.''' {{smaller|See ''transcendental.''}} ='''Syn.''' {{smaller|2. ''Theme, Point,'' etc. See ''subject.''}} ¶ '''topical''' (top′i-ka̤l), ''a.'' [< ''topic'' + ''-al.''] 1. Of or pertaining to a place or locality; especially, limited to a particular spot; local. {{smaller block|The men of Archenfeld in Herefordshire claimed by custom to lead the van-guard; but surely this priviledge was ''topical,'' and confined to the Welsh wars. {{right|''Fuller,'' Worthies, II. 145.}}}} {{smaller block|He was now intending to visite Staffordshire, and, as he had of Oxfordshire, to give us the natural, ''topical,'' political, and mechanical history. ''Evelyn,'' Diary, July 8, 1675.}} {{smaller block|The ''topical'' application of the artificial alizarine colours. {{right|''Workshop Receipts'', 2d ser., p. 215.}}}} 2. Specifically, in ''med.'', pertaining or applied to a particular part of the body; local. {{smaller block|He is robust and healthy, and his change of colour was not accompanied with any sensible disease, either general or ''topical''. {{right|''Jefferson'', Notes on Virginia (1787), p. 120.}} For the most part, however, in this country, physicians have abandoned severe ''topical'' measures, limiting themselves to antiseptic and soothing applications. {{right|''Austin Flint'', Diphtheria (Amer. Cyc.).}}}} 3. Pertaining to or proceeding from a topic, or category of arguments; hence, merely probable, as an argument. {{smaller block|Evidences of fact can be no more than ''topical'' and probable. {{right|''Sir M. Hale.''}}}} 4. Pertaining to a subject of discourse, composition, or the like; concerned with a particular topic; specifically, dealing with topics of current or local interest. {{smaller block|Conversation . . . was . . . ever taking new turns, branching into ''topical'' surprises, and at all turns and on every topic was luminous, high, edifying, full. {{right|''J. Morley'', Burke, p. 120.}} The music-hall with beer and tobacco, the comic man bawling a ''topical'' song and executing the famous clog dance. {{right|''Contemporary Rev.'', LI. 227.}}}} {{smaller|'''Topical coloring''', in ''calico-printing'', the application of color to limited and determined parts of the cloth, as distinguished from the dyeing of the whole.—'''Topical resultant.''' See ''resultant''.}} '''topically''' (top′i-kal-i), ''adv.'' With reference to topics; also, with regard or application to a particular place, spot, subject, etc. {{smaller block|The various collections have been scientifically and ''topically'' classified and arranged. {{right|''Pop. Sci. Mo.'', XXVIII. 717.}}}} '''topic-folio†''' (top′ik-fō″liō), ''n.'' A commonplace-book. {{smaller block|An English concordance and a ''topic folio'', the gatherings and savings of a sober graduatship, a Harmony and a Catena, treading the constant round of certain common doctrinall heads. {{right|''Milton'', Areopagitica.}}}} '''topinch†''' (tö-pinch′), ''v. t.'' [A sham word, invented by editors of Shakspere as a compound of ''to-'', intensive, + ''pinch'', and defined "to pinch severely." The proper reading is simply ''to pinch.'' Instances of ''to'' with an infinitive after ''let'' occur in Shakspere elsewhere (Hamlet, iv. 6. 11), and instances of ''to'' with an infinitive after other verbs with which ''to'' does not now usually appear abound in Shakspere and his contemporaries. The prefix ''to-'', on the other hand, was obsolete in Shakspere's time, and it was never used "intensively" in such a sense as 'severely.'] An erroneous form of ''to pinch.'' See the etymology. {{smaller block|Then let them all encircle him about, And, fairy-like, ''topinch'' the unclean knight. {{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iv. 4. 57.}}}} '''topknot''' (top′not), ''n.'' 1. Any knot, tuft, or crest worn or growing on the head: applied to any egret, crest, or tuft of feathers on the head of a bird, the hair on the top of the human head, any projecting or conspicuous ornament for the head, etc.; specifically, a bow, as of ribbon, forming a part of the head-dress of women in the seventeenth century. {{smaller block|We had that, among other laudable fashions, from London. I think it came over with your mode of wearing high ''topknots.'' {{right|''Farquhar'', Love and a Bottle, i. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|It is undoubtedly from hence [the Danish language] that the Bride-Favours, or the ''Top-Knots'' at Marriages, which were considered as Emblems of the Ties of Duty and Affection between the Bride and her Spouse, have been derived. {{right|''Bourne's Pop. Antiq.'' (1777), p. 349.}}}} {{smaller block|That fine gentleman . . . whose thick ''topknot'' of wavy hair . . . and general air of worldly exaltation . . . were painfully suggestive to Lyddy of Herod, Pontius Pilate, or the much-quoted Gallio. {{right|''George Eliot'', Felix Holt, xxxviii.}}}} 2. A flatfish, ''Phrynorhombus unimaculatus'', or Bloch's topknot, and some related species: so called from a long filament on the head. {{smaller|Some of the topknots are of the same genus as the turbot, as Eckstrom's, ''Rhombus norvegicus'', and Müller's, ''R. punctatus.''}} 3. One of any of the breeds of domestic hens which have a crest.—'''Miller's topknot.''' {{smaller|Same as ''smear-dab.''}} '''topknotted''' (top′not″ed), ''a.'' Adorned with bows and topknots. Having a high top; hence, figuratively, pompous; bombastic; inflated; pretentious: as, ''toplofty'' airs; ''toplofty'' speeches. [Colloq., U. S.] '''top-mall''' (top′mâl), ''n.'' See ''mall''1. In a man-of-war the topmen are divided into fore-, main-, and mizzen-topmen. Also ''topsman.''—3. A merchant vessel. ''Halliwell.''
